items.en: I am writing a letter to my mum.
This is a letter of the alphabet.
The garden is behind the house.
The cat is under the chair.
My wallet is in my pocket.
There is an apple on the table.
What time do you go to work?
The bird is in the sky.
The Sun is very far from the Earth.
There are islands in the sea.
A big ship needs a big sea.
There are many trees in the forest.
There are flowers in the field.
A goose is a water bird.
There is a metro in Kazan.
Kazan is the capital of Tatarstan.
There are many people in the park.
Are you going to town today?
He is not in the city.
My car is in bad shape.
This language is hard to understand.
There are few Tatar websites on the Internet.
My language isn't on the list!
The office is on the right.
He has a lot of money.
You don't have a lot of money.
How much free time do you have?
There is no life without air.
He has a lot of experience.
Does it have gelatine in it?
There is one apple on the table.
Will you tell me or not?
The dog isn't sleeping, it's playing.
She is a very beautiful woman.
A nightingale won't sing in a cage.

a1-greetings.title: Greetings and Politeness
a1-greetings.pattern: Сәлам! · Хәерле иртә! · Рәхмәт! · Сау бул! / Сау булыгыз!
a1-greetings.explanation: Tatar greetings are short and warm. Сәлам (hello) works almost everywhere; Хәерле иртә / көн / кич wish someone a good morning, day or evening. Many polite words have two forms: a plain one for one friend (Сау бул!, Рәхим ит!) and one with -ыгыз/-егез for several people or anyone you address politely (Сау булыгыз!, Гафу итегез).
a1-greetings.fact: Tatar is a Turkic language spoken by several million people. It is an official language of the Republic of Tatarstan alongside Russian, and its closest relative is Bashkir.

a1-pronouns.title: I, You, He: Personal Pronouns
a1-pronouns.pattern: мин · син · ул · без · сез · алар
a1-pronouns.explanation: The pronouns are мин (I), син (you, one friend), ул (he, she or it — Tatar has no gender), без (we), сез (you, several people or polite) and алар (they). In everyday speech the word for am/is/are is simply left out: Мин студент — I (am a) student. Ул татар — He (is a) Tatar.
a1-pronouns.fact: Because ул means both he and she, Tatar sentences never tell you a person's gender through the pronoun — context does that job.

a1-possessive.title: My Mother, Your Father: Possessive Endings
a1-possessive.pattern: минем әни-ем · синең әти-ең · аның кыз-ы · безнең әти
a1-possessive.explanation: Possession is marked twice: by a pronoun (минем my, синең your, аның his/her, безнең our) and by an ending on the noun: -ым/-ем for my, -ың/-ең for your, -ы/-е for his/her. The pronoun can be dropped because the ending already says it all: Әнием белми — my mum doesn't know.
a1-possessive.fact: Tatar words have vowel harmony: words with back vowels (а, о, у, ы) take back-vowel endings like -ым, and words with front vowels (ә, ө, ү, е, и) take front ones like -ем.

a1-this.title: This Is…: Бу and Questions with -мы
a1-this.pattern: Бу нәрсә? · Бу — китап. · Бу мәче-ме?
a1-this.explanation: Бу means this and ул means that. To say what something is, just put the two words side by side: Бу китап — this (is a) book. To turn a statement into a yes/no question, add -мы or -ме to the word you ask about: Бу мәче — this is a cat; Бу мәчеме? — is this a cat?
a1-this.fact: The dash in Бу — китап is only punctuation. It marks the missing is and is often left out in writing.

a1-locative.title: Where Things Are: -да/-дә, -та/-тә
a1-locative.explanation: The ending -да/-дә (after voiceless consonants -та/-тә) means in, at or on: өйдә — at home, Казанда — in Kazan, паркта — in the park. Words like артында (behind) and астында (under) follow the noun: өй артында — behind the house, урындык астында — under the chair.
a1-locative.fact: Кайда means where (at what place) and кая means where to — but in everyday speech кая is also often used for where.

a1-present.title: I Read, You Write: The Present Tense
a1-present.explanation: The present tense adds -а/-ә (or -ый/-и after vowels) to the verb and then a personal ending: -м (I), -сың/-сең (you), nothing (he/she), -быз/-без (we), -сыз/-сез (you all), -лар/-ләр (they). Язам — I write, язасыз — you (all) write, яза — he writes. The negative uses -мый/-ми: язмыйм — I don't write.
a1-present.fact: This one tense covers both I write and I am writing: Мин язам can mean either, and context decides.

a1-numbers.title: Numbers, Age and Time
a1-numbers.pattern: бер · ике · өч · дүрт · биш · алты · җиде · сигез · тугыз · ун
a1-numbers.explanation: The numbers one to ten are бер, ике, өч, дүрт, биш, алты, җиде, сигез, тугыз, ун; eleven is ун бер (written унбер), eighteen is унсигез. After a number the noun stays singular: ике мәче — two cats. Age uses the dative: Миңа ун яшь — I am ten (lit. to me ten years). The time is сәгать: Сәгать ничә? — What time is it?
a1-numbers.fact: Tatar counts like the other Turkic languages: ун бер is literally ten one, and егерме бер is twenty one.

a1-have.title: Having: бар and юк
a1-have.pattern: минем мәчем бар · аның эте бар · акчам юк · …бармы?
a1-have.explanation: Tatar has no verb to have. Instead it says my cat exists: Минем мәчем бар — I have a cat (lit. my cat there is). Юк means there isn't: Акчам юк — I have no money. Ask with бармы: Ручкагыз бармы? — Do you have a pen?
a1-have.fact: The same бар/юк pair also means there is / there isn't on its own: Монда балалар бар — There are children here.

a1-negation.title: Saying No: түгел, юк, -ма
a1-negation.pattern: Мин табиб түгел · Ул өйдә юк · Елама! · Аңламыйм
a1-negation.explanation: Tatar has several ways to say no. Түгел negates a description: Мин табиб түгел — I'm not a doctor. Юк says something isn't there. Verbs take -ма/-мә in commands (Елама! — Don't cry!) and -мый/-ми in the present tense (Аңламыйм — I don't understand).
a1-negation.fact: Начар түгел (lit. not bad) is a common modest way to say something is good.

a1-questions.title: Asking Questions
a1-questions.pattern: кем · нәрсә · кайда · кая · ничек · ничә · кайчан · нигә · …мы/-ме
a1-questions.explanation: Question words stay where the answer would be: Ул кем? — Who is he? Сез кайда яшисез? — Where do you live? For yes/no questions add -мы/-ме to the key word: Сез ялгызмы? — Are you alone? The word order doesn't change.
a1-questions.fact: Нәрсә (what) is often shortened to ни in set phrases, as in Ни хәлләр? — How are things?

a1-imperative.title: Asking and Telling: the Imperative
a1-imperative.pattern: кил · килегез · бир · бирегез · әйдә · әйдәгез
a1-imperative.explanation: The bare verb is a command to one friend: Кил! — Come! Бир! — Give! Adding -ыгыз/-егез makes it plural or polite: Килегез! Керегез! Әйдә / әйдәгез means come on, let's go. Add зинһар to make any request softer: Зинһар, гафу ит!
a1-imperative.fact: Әле after a command softens it, like just: Газета бир әле — Just give me the paper.

dialogue.en: Thank you! Your home is very beautiful.

a1-dative.title: Going Places: -га/-гә, -ка/-кә
a1-dative.explanation: The ending -га/-гә (after voiceless consonants -ка/-кә) shows where you are going or who receives something: шәһәргә — to town, эшкә — to work, мәктәпкә — to school, Әниемә хат язам — I'm writing a letter to my mum. Кая барасыз? — Where are you going?
a1-dative.fact: Personal pronouns change in the dative: мин → миңа, син → сиңа, ул → аңа.
